questions.q: In the 'Waiter' analogy for how APIs work, what does 'the Kitchen' represent?
options: The user's web browser
The Server and its Database -- where the actual work happens and data is stored
The API documentation
The HTTP request itself

questions.q: Which HTTP method maps to the 'Create' action in CRUD, sending data to the server to make a new record?
options: GET
POST
DELETE
PUT
Converts a raw JSON text string back into a usable JavaScript object
Converts a usable JavaScript object into a raw string of JSON text so it can be transmitted over a network
Deletes all the data in an object
Checks if a string is valid JSON

questions.q: Why is the fetch() command in JavaScript considered 'Asynchronous'?
options: It only works once per page load
It runs in the background, allowing the rest of the website to load while waiting for the server's response, instead of freezing the browser
It requires a special asynchronous internet connection
It only fetches images, not text data

questions.q: If you write const data = fetch('url') WITHOUT using the await keyword, what does the variable 'data' actually contain?
options: The actual JSON data from the server
A Pending Promise, not the real data yet
An error message
undefined, with no further information

questions.q: What does the await keyword do when placed before response.json()?
options: It deletes the response after reading it
It pauses the function until the raw text response finishes converting into a usable JavaScript object, instead of returning a pending Promise
It converts the response into an image
It sends a second request automatically

ch13_lab_security.title: Quick Check: API Security & Error Handling

questions.q: Why should you NEVER expose a private API key (like a client's payment key) directly in your front-end JavaScript?
options: It will make the page load slower
Anyone can view your JS code in DevTools, steal the key, and rack up charges or cause damage on the client's account
Front-end JavaScript can't use API keys at all
It will cause a CSS styling conflict

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a try/catch block around a fetch() request?
options: It makes the request run faster
It provides a safety net that catches errors (like no Wi-Fi) without crashing the entire application
It automatically retries failed requests forever
It hides the request from the browser console

questions.q: If response.ok returns false after a fetch() call (e.g., the server replied with a 404), what should your code do next?
options: Nothing -- fetch already threw an error automatically
Manually throw an error so the catch block can handle the failure gracefully
Immediately reload the whole page
Ignore it and use the data anyway
